content_voiceover: This slide compares a normal type A reaction with one distorted by cold agglutinin interference. On the left, the clean control pattern shows Anti-A 4 plus, Anti-B negative, Anti-D positive, and a negative control tube. On the right, interference muddies everything, Anti-A 4 plus, Anti-B an unexpected 3 plus, Anti-D 4 plus, and critically, the control tube itself is positive at 4 plus. That control tube contains only the patient's red cells with no added antibody, so a positive reaction there means the cells are auto-agglutinating, not truly reacting with reagent. This is the single biggest clue you're dealing with interference rather than a real antigen-antibody reaction. Two fixes resolve it, the prewarm technique, warming samples and reagents to eliminate weak cold-reactive binding, and treating the sample with DTT, dithiothreitol, a reducing agent that breaks the disulfide bonds holding IgM pentamers together and eliminates IgM-mediated agglutination.
keypoints: A positive control tube, patient cells alone reacting, signals auto-agglutination not a true reaction
Cold agglutinin interference causes unexpected reactivity in Anti-B and reverse typing cells
Prewarm technique is first-line to eliminate weak cold-reactive interference
DTT, dithiothreitol, is a reducing agent that disrupts IgM pentamers for refractory cases
keypoint_voiceover: High-yield point, a positive control tube with only the patient's own cells means auto-agglutination, not a true reaction, that's your tip-off for cold agglutinin interference. Two fixes, prewarming resolves most cases by eliminating weak cold-reactive binding, and DTT, a reducing agent, breaks the disulfide bonds of IgM pentamers for the tougher cases.
